extracted.intended_audience: general public and legal community interested in judicial decision-making
extracted.subtask_description: A short public-facing talk summarizing behavioural-science and social-psychology research on how judges decide, aimed at exposing non-legal influences on judicial outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, judges’ decisions should always be impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative ideal invoked by the talk (e.g., ‘Lady Justice’ wears a blindfold and carefully balances the scales of justice). Used as a benchmark against which real-world judicial behaviour is contrasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The talk contrasts the ideal of rational decision-making with evidence that judges may commit reasoning errors; rationality serves as an evaluative standard for decision quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbiasedness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as part of the ideal trio (impartial, rational and unbiased); the talk highlights research showing biases can nevertheless influence outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of psychological errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological errors may affect judicial outcomes and therefore should be identified and minimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The talk reports 'psychological errors' identified by behavioural science and social psychology as sources of flawed judicial decision-making; awareness and corrective measures are implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence in numerical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor numerical reasoning can bear on judicial outcomes and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker flags 'poor numerical reasoning' as a concrete cognitive vulnerability that can affect judges; implies importance of quantitative literacy in judging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional regulation (avoid excessive emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive emotion may influence judicial outcomes and should be controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The talk names 'excessive emotion' as a factor that can sway decisions, suggesting emotional control is a criterion of sound judicial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of non-legal influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors other than law (psychological, institutional and political forces) affect judges when they make decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker's research investigates these non-legal forces; good judicial practice includes recognizing and accounting for institutional and political pressures as well as cognitive influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical behavioural-science methods to evaluate judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical research from behavioural science and social psychology can and should be used to study judicial decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The talk emphasizes 'research that “judges the judges”' and the speaker is writing a book that 'assimilates and analyses global research' — implying that systematic empirical study is the appropriate method to assess and improve judging.
